October 6, 2026


        Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary                                                                             via eFiling
        Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
        888 First Street N.E.
        Washington, DC 20426

        Re:      NorthWestern Corporation, Docket Nos.                  ER18-2511-011
                                                                        EL26-89-000

                 Response to Show Cause Order


        Dear Secretary Reese:

        Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”) “Order on
        Notice of Change in Status, Instituting Section 206 Proceeding, and Establishing Refund Effective
        Date,” issued on August 7, 2026 (“Show Cause Order”) in the above-captioned dockets,1
        NorthWestern Corporation d/b/a NorthWestern Energy (“NorthWestern”) hereby shows cause as
        to why the Commission should not revoke NorthWestern’s market-based rate authority in the
        NorthWestern (“NWMT”) balancing authority area (“BAA”).

        As further described below and in accordance with FERC Order No. 697,2 NorthWestern has
        previously submitted a Delivered Price Test (“DPT”) to rebut the presumption of market power
        due to limited failures of the wholesale market share screens. NorthWestern reiterates its intent
        to rely upon the findings of the previously submitted DPT, as revised herein, and asks that the
        Commission find that it has successfully rebutted the presumption of market power in the
        NWMT BAA via the analysis presented in the DPT.3




        1 NorthWestern Corporation, 196 FERC ¶ 61,113 (2026).
        2 E.g., Order No. 697 at P 63 (“The rebuttable presumption of horizontal market power that attaches to sellers failing

        one of the indicative screens is just that—a rebuttable presumption. It is not a definitive finding by the Commission;
        sellers are provided with several procedural options including the right to challenge the market power presumption
        by submitting a [Delivered Price Test] analysis. . . .”).
        3 Attached is the Affidavit of Julie R. Solomon (“Solomon Affidavit”), including Exhibits SEC-1 through SEC-5. Ms.

        Solomon made minor updates to her DPT analysis; however, those updates do not change her conclusion that
        NorthWestern lacks market power. The updates are discussed in the Solomon Affidavit.


208 N. Montana Avenue, Suite 200 | Helena, MT 59601                                                 NorthWesternEnergy.com
         I.       Background

        On April 30, 2026, NorthWestern submitted a Notice of Change in Status Filing (“April Filing”) to
        report new affiliation with more than 100 megawatts (MW) of generation capacity in the
        Northwest region. The April Filing included a market power analysis for the study period of
        December 1, 2022, through November 30, 2023 (“Study Period”). NorthWestern stated that it
        passed the pivotal supplier indicative screen but failed the wholesale market share analysis in
        the NWMT BAA in two seasons. Consistent with the Commission’s orders on market-based
        rates,4 Julie R. Solomon, the Managing Director at Secretariat Economists LLC and an
        experienced utility consultant, conducted a DPT. As Ms. Solomon’s revised DPT analysis
        indicates, NorthWestern meets the Commission’s requirements for an entity to demonstrate a
        sufficiently competitive destination market and obtain market-based rate authority for that
        destination market, thereby rebutting the presumption of market power in the NWMT BAA. As
        noted, the Commission issued its Show Cause Order on August 7, 2026, providing 60 days for
        NorthWestern to respond.


        II.      Response to Show Cause Order

        The Show Cause Order indicates that the Commission, as is its standard practice, instituted its
        section 206 proceeding solely based on the market share indicative screen failures and has not
        yet reviewed the materials submitted in April 2026.5 NorthWestern respectfully submits that, the
        DPT and the supporting analysis provided by Ms. Solomon in the April Filing, as revised herein,
        as well as this response, sufficiently rebut the presumption of horizontal market power in the
        NWMT BAA. The Commission should reaffirm that NorthWestern does not have market power in
        the NWMT BAA and should not revoke or otherwise condition NorthWestern’s market-based
        rate authority for sales in the NWMT BAA.

        The Commission provides certain safe-harbor thresholds for applicants to pass the DPT screen.
        The safe-harbor threshold for the Market Share Test and the Market Concentration Test is a
        market share of less than 20 percent and a market Hirschman-Herfindahl Index (“HHI”) of less
        than 2,500 points.6 These metrics must be evaluated for both the Economic Capacity (“EC”)
        (which ignores load obligations), and Available Economic Capacity (“AEC”) (essentially, economic
        supply in excess of load-serving obligations), although AEC is clearly the more relevant metric
        for a load-serving entity in a largely “non-restructured” market. Montana has “limited” retail
        access and NorthWestern has wholesale and retail load obligations.

        4 Id. at PP 63, 74-75, 105.

        5 Show Cause Order at P 2 & n.7.

        6 Order No. 697 at PP 104-17.




Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary | October 6, 2026 | Page 2                        NorthWesternEnergy.com
         The results of Ms. Solomon’s DPT analysis for the NWMT BAA under the AEC measure are

                           Table 1: DPT Results (Available Economic Capacity) (NWMT)




        As shown in the table above and the Solomon Affidavit,7 NorthWestern’s market shares are

        it terminated a section 206 investigation of MBR authority of another entity with three market
        share failures, stating: "[w]hile the base case analysis indicates that the Sellers' market share
        under the available economic capacity measure exceeds 20% in three season/load periods, the
        corresponding market concentration levels in these periods range between 359 and 1,714, which
        are below the Commission's HHI threshold of 2,500."8 Moreover, the market share thresholds
        that are above 20% are below market share values that the Commission has previously
        accepted.9 Market concentration, as measured by the HHI, ranges from approximately 700 to
        1,300 points including for the sensitivities and thus is well below the 2,500 point threshold.

        Ms. Solomon also prepared a DPT analysis for EC in which the Pivotal Supplier Test is passed in
        all periods for EC at base prices and price sensitivities. Market shares range from approximately

        8 Tucson Elec. Power Co., 194 FERC ¶ 61,011, at P 30 (2026).

        9 E.g., id. (accepting DPT screen failures of 37%, 36%, and 25%); Tucson Elec. Power Co., 183 FERC ¶ 61,063 (2023)

        (accepting DPT screen failures of 23% and 27%).


Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary | October 6, 2026 | Page 3                                          NorthWesternEnergy.com
         38 to 45 percent.10 The Market Concentration Test is passed on all periods, with HHIs below
        2,500 points.11 Although NorthWestern does not pass all of the DPT metrics for EC, such results
        are not a reliable assessment of NorthWestern’s actual market power in the NWMT BAA given
        their load-serving obligations in NWMT, as outlined in Commission Order No. 697.12

        The Commission has stated that a review of actual sales data in the relevant market is a useful
        tool.13 Historical sales data provide additional support for the conclusion that NorthWestern
        lacks market power in the NWMT BAA. As shown in the Solomon Affidavit,14 NorthWestern’s
        share of quarterly sales based on data reported in the Commission’s EQRs in the NWMT BAA for
        the 2020-2025 period ranged from below 20 percent to a high of 36 percent, on a quarterly
        basis. For the same period, market concentration ranged from about 1,200 points to a high of
        2,700 points quarterly, but overall annual average HHI was below 2,000 points.

        In addition, NorthWestern resubmits the Affidavit of Joe Stimatz, Supply and Transmission
        Services Officer at NorthWestern, which explains the operational and resource adequacy
        considerations underlying NorthWestern’s increased ownership interest in Colstrip. As Mr.
        Stimatz explains, the Colstrip shares acquired from Avista are held directly by NorthWestern and
        are intended to serve the Company’s Montana electric load by providing dependable,
        dispatchable capacity, particularly during winter peak conditions. The additional owned capacity
        strengthens NorthWestern’s resource adequacy position and reduces reliance on short-term
        market purchases during stressed system conditions, rather than facilitating speculative
        wholesale sales. Accordingly, the changes described in this filing reflect prudent supply planning
        by a load-serving utility and do not represent a material departure from the characteristics on
        which the Commission previously relied in granting NorthWestern market-based rate authority.


        III.     Conclusion

        NorthWestern respectfully submits that the analytical results presented successfully rebut the
        presumption of market power in the NWMT BAA. Accordingly, the Commission should not

                               AFFIDAVIT OF JOE STIMATZ

1. My name is Joe Stimatz and I am the Supply and Transmission Services Officer at

   NorthWestern Corporation d/b/a NorthWestern Energy (“NorthWestern” or “Company”). My

   business address is 11 E Park Street, Butte, Montana 59701.

2. The purpose of this affidavit is to provide information in support of NorthWestern’s change in

   status report for the NWMT Balancing Authority Area (“BAA”) filed with the Federal Energy

   Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) in the above-referenced docket.

                                        BACKGROUND

3. I have been employed by NorthWestern for approximately fifteen years and currently serve as

   Supply and Transmission Services Officer, a position I assumed in February 2026. In this role,

   I provide executive oversight of NorthWestern’s electric and natural gas supply functions, with

   primary responsibility for ensuring reliable and cost‑effective service to the company’s electric

   utility customers, including oversight of power procurement, electricity and natural gas

   trading, and coordination of supply‑side operations. From September 2022 through February

   2026, I served as Director of Market Operations, and from 2011 to 2022, I was Manager of

   Asset Optimization, during which time I was responsible for managing and optimizing

   NorthWestern’s     electricity   supply   portfolio   and    supporting    long‑term    resource

   decision‑making. I have extensive experience managing utility supply activities and assessing

   market conditions. I hold a Bachelor of Arts degree in Finance from Gonzaga University, a

                                                1
    Master of Business Administration from the University of Montana, and am a Chartered

   Financial Analyst (“CFA”). Prior to joining NorthWestern, I gained experience in electric

   power markets and portfolio management through roles with power marketers and energy

   trading organizations, including positions involving origination, pricing, risk management, and

   asset valuation.

4. NorthWestern is a public utility engaged in the generation, transmission, and distribution of

   electricity and the supply and transportation of natural gas. NorthWestern’s service territory

   includes communities and surrounding rural areas covering two-thirds of Montana and

   Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming.

5. NorthWestern plans its supply portfolio to ensure that sufficient firm capacity is available to

   meet customer demand during peak conditions, including periods of extreme weather or system

   stress. Montana’s electric system is particularly sensitive to winter reliability conditions, when

   high loads coincide with limited market liquidity and constrained transmission availability.

   For these reasons, NorthWestern places a high value on dependable, dispatchable generation

   resources that can be counted on to perform during such periods.

                 USE OF AVISTA COLSTRIP SHARES TO SERVE LOAD

6. The Colstrip Generating Station (“Colstrip”) in Eastern Montana has long been an important

   component of NorthWestern’s resource portfolio because it provides firm, baseload capacity

   that is available independent of short‑term market conditions. Unlike market purchases, which

   may be unavailable or subject to significant price volatility during tight system conditions,

   owned generation such as shares of Colstrip provide NorthWestern with greater operational

   certainty and control. Ownership is particularly important during winter peak periods, when

   reliance on external market supplies can expose customers to higher costs and increased

   reliability risk.
                                                 2
 7. Colstrip is a four-unit coal-fired generation plant. Units 1 and 2 were retired in 2020. Units 3

   and 4 remain operational. Until January 1, 2026, six different companies held ownership

   interests in Colstrip Units 3 and 4:

8. Due to changes in state law, Puget and Avista were required to terminate their ownership in

   Colstrip Units 3 and 4. NorthWestern acquired Avista’s ownership share effective January 1,

   2026. An affiliate of NorthWestern, NorthWestern Colstrip 370Pu LLC (NorthWestern

   Colstrip), acquired Puget’s ownership share also effective January 1, 2026. As a result, the

   current ownership shares are as follows:

                                    Owner                    Unit 3    Unit 4
                    NorthWestern Colstrip (acquired
                                                              25%       25%
                    Puget share)
                    NorthWestern (acquired Avista
                                                              15%       15%
                    share)
                    PGE                                       20%       20%
                    PAC                                       10%       10%
                    NorthWestern                                        30%
                   Talen                                   30%
9. The Colstrip shares acquired from Avista and held directly by NorthWestern are intended to

   be used to support electric service to NorthWestern’s Montana customers. These shares

   increase the amount of owned capacity that NorthWestern can rely upon to meet peak load and


                                                3
    planning reserve requirements. From a resource adequacy perspective, the additional Colstrip

   capacity contributes to a more balanced and resilient supply portfolio and reduces the need to

   procure incremental capacity or energy from the market to meet load obligations.

10. Ownership of additional Colstrip capacity enables NorthWestern to reduce its dependence on

   short‑term and spot market purchases, particularly during periods when such purchases may

   be scarce or expensive. While wholesale market transactions remain an important tool for

   balancing the system on a day‑to‑day basis, NorthWestern does not rely on the short-term

   market as a substitute for long‑term resource planning. Instead, the acquisition of the Avista

   Colstrip shares allows NorthWestern to internalize a greater portion of its supply needs,

   thereby reducing exposure to market price volatility and supply availability risk.

11. NorthWestern’s participation in the Western Resource Adequacy Program (“WRAP”) further

   underscores the importance of maintaining sufficient owned and controllable generation

   resources to serve load. Participation in WRAP requires NorthWestern to demonstrate that it

   has adequate qualifying resources available to meet its forecasted peak demand and reserve

   margin obligations during periods of system stress. These requirements specify the need for

   dependable, dispatchable capacity that can be relied upon during critical operating conditions,

   rather than capacity that must be obtained through short‑term market purchases.

   NorthWestern’s ownership of firm resources such as Colstrip—including the Avista shares

   acquired and held for load service—directly supports its ability to meet WRAP obligations and

   reinforces prudent long‑term resource adequacy planning consistent with its role as a

   load‑serving utility.

12. The Colstrip capacity acquired from Avista thus is operationally distinct from generation assets

   intended for wholesale marketing purposes.         These shares are not acquired to expand



                                                 4
    speculative or merchant sales activity. Rather, they are integrated into NorthWestern’s supply

   strategy as a means of serving native load more reliably and economically. Any incidental

   wholesale sales that may occur are secondary to, and driven by, the operational needs of

   serving load rather than a shift in NorthWestern’s underlying business model.

                                         CONCLUSION

13. In my professional judgment, NorthWestern’s increased ownership interest in Colstrip,

   including the Avista shares, is consistent with its longstanding role as a load‑serving utility in

   Montana.    The acquisition strengthens NorthWestern’s resource adequacy position and

   improves its ability to plan for future load needs without undue reliance on external market

   transactions. These changes do not reflect an expansion of market power or a material

   departure from the characteristics on which the Commission previously relied in granting

   NorthWestern market‑based rate authority.

14. This concludes my Affidavit.

                                  AFFIDAVIT OF JULIE R. SOLOMON

INTRODUCTION

          My name is Julie R. Solomon. I am a Managing Director at Secretariat, an economic
consulting firm located at 2121 K Street, NW, Washington, DC. A large portion of my consulting
activities involves electric utility industry restructuring and the transition from regulation to
competition. I have been involved extensively in consulting on market power issues concerning
mergers, other asset transactions, and market-based rate applications. I often file affidavits before
the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) in connection with electric utility
mergers, the purchase and sale of jurisdictional assets, applications for market-based rates, and
triennial updates. My resume is included as Exhibit SEC-1.

          I previously have submitted affidavits in connection with triennial and change-in-status
filings on behalf of NorthWestern Corporation (“NorthWestern” or “Seller”), presenting indicative
screens and, where necessary, Delivered Price Test (“DPT”) analyses in compliance with the
Commission’s guidelines contained in Order No. 697,1 Order No. 816,2 and Order No. 860.3
Included among those is a change in status filing submitted April 30, 2026 in Docket No. ER18-

      No. 697-A, FERC Stats. & Regs ¶ 31,268, order on reh’g and clarification, 124 FERC ¶ 61,055, order on reh'g and

 2511-011 (“April 2026 CIS”), for which I provided market-based rate screens and included a DPT
analysis.

        On August 7, 2026, the Commission issued an order in that docket instituting a section 206
proceeding and establishing a refund effective date. The order requires NorthWestern to file a
response as to why the Commission should not revoke its market-based rate authority in the NWMT
balancing authority area (“BAA”). I have been asked to provide an analysis in support of
NorthWestern’s response to the Commission’s order, which includes both a DPT and a discussion
of other relevant facts. Exhibit SEC-2 reports NorthWestern’s generation and long-term power
purchase/sale commitments.

        Consistent with the April 2026 CIS filing, my analysis is driven by NorthWestern’s recent
acquisition of, and affiliation with, additional shares of the Colstrip Plant; specifically, a 222 MW
share acquired from Avista Corporation; and a 370 MW share acquired by NorthWestern’s affiliate,
NorthWestern Colstrip 370Pu LLC, from Puget Sound Energy. The 370 MW acquired from Puget
Sound Energy remains subject to a long-term sales agreement with Mercuria Energy America, LLC
(“Mercuria”); thus, the net MWs relevant to the change-in-status arise from the 222 MW share
acquired from Avista Corporation.

        The DPT analysis is based on the study period (December 2022-November 2023) that was
used in connection with NorthWestern’s pending Northwest Region triennial and is the study period
for which a DPT was submitted in June 2025. The DPT analysis is limited to the NWMT BAA,
where the indicative screens were failed. The DPT submitted here includes minor updates to the
analysis submitted with the April 2026 CIS.4

        The DPT analysis for the NWMT market results in (1) metrics that fall within the range that
the Commission has accepted in finding parties have met the appropriate market power standards in
other market-based rate proceedings (including under section 206, as discussed below); and (2)
metrics that are within the Commission’s safe-harbor thresholds for passing the DPT Market Share

    with Invenergy for the output of Judith Gap Wind Farm that expires December 31, 2026, and hence it is no longer
    considered a long-term contract. The long-term purchase from Powerex remains in place until the end of 2027 and
    thus continues to be treated as a long-term contract. The two long-term contracts sales from Colstrip with Mercuria

    future or ‘imminent changes’ such as the future expiration of a long-term contract would be excessively burdensome

 and Market Concentration Tests, as discussed below. I also provide Electric Quarterly Report
(“EQR”) data that indicate, on average, NorthWestern’s reported annual EQR sales in NWMT are
approximately 22 percent for the period 2020-2025 (and market concentration, on average, is less
than 2,000 points).

DPT ANALYSIS

          Under Order No. 697, the failure of either indicative screen creates a rebuttable presumption
that the seller has generation market power. Consistent with Commission guidance that such
presumption can be rebutted through a DPT and other evidence based on historical sales information,
I submit herein a DPT and other relevant evidence. The assumptions underlying the DPT are
included in Exhibit SEC-3 (“Data and Methods”).5

          The Commission provides certain safe-harbor thresholds for applicants to pass the DPT
screen. Specifically, the Commission established a safe-harbor threshold of pass/fail for the Pivotal
Supplier Test for each of the ten DPT periods. The safe-harbor threshold for the Market Share Test
and the Market Concentration Test are a market share of less than 20 percent and a market HHI of
less than 2,500 points.6 These metrics must be evaluated for both the Economic Capacity (“EC”)
(which ignores load obligations), and Available Economic Capacity (“AEC”) (essentially, economic
supply in excess of load-serving obligations), although AEC is clearly the more relevant metric for
a load-serving entity in a largely “non-restructured” market, as is the case for NorthWestern.
Montana has “limited” retail access and NorthWestern has wholesale and retail load obligations.
Notably, the Commission generally has not treated the DPT results as bright-line results, and has
exercised some latitude, taking into consideration certain other factors addressed in more detail
herein.

          AEC is comprised of (a) internal generation that is economic and excess after meeting native
load obligations, and (b) external supply that also meets the economics of the DPT and can be

 imported into the market. Under the EC and AEC measures, energy production capability that is
attributed to a market participant is the capacity controlled by the market participant that can reach
the destination market, taking transmission constraints and costs into account, at a variable cost no
higher than 105 percent of the destination market price. The Market Share Test and the Market
Concentration Test are direct outputs of the DPT. The Pivotal Supplier Test is implemented in the
following manner: (i) for the EC measure, the test is whether load in NWMT can be met without
capacity owned or controlled by NorthWestern in NWMT. For the AEC analysis, the proxy for
wholesale load calculated in Pivotal Supplier Analysis indicative screen (i.e., needle peak less the
daily average peak for the peak month) is shaped into the ten time periods based on overall load in
NWMT.

        The results of the DPT analyses for NWMT are reported in Exhibit SEC-4 and SEC-5 for
AEC and EC, respectively. The results for the DPT analysis based on the AEC measure at base
prices are reported in Table 1 below, which is arguably the more relevant metric given that
NorthWestern is a load-serving entity in a largely “non-restructured” market. As shown in Table 1
below, market shares are below the 20 percent threshold in half of the time periods, whereas the HHI
in each of the ten periods is well below the 2,500 point threshold.7

                    Data and Methods for Delivered Price Test (“DPT”)

        This exhibit describes data and assumptions used in the delivered price test study
(“study”). The data supporting the study are provided in electronic workpapers. Section I
describes the time periods used in the study. Section II describes the relevant geographic
market and balancing authority areas. Section III describes relevant generation resources,

I.      Periods
        The study calculates market shares and market concentration for ten representative
periods during the year consistent with the Commission’s requirements. 1 The year is divided
into three seasons (spring/fall, summer and winter), and each season is divided into three or
four periods based on NERC on-peak/off-peak definition and peak load levels. The seasons
are Spring/Fall, Summer, and Winter. For Spring/Fall and Winter, the market conditions
correspond to (1) the Top 10% of on-peak load hours for the season, (2) the remaining on-peak
load hours, and (3) off-peak hours. For Summer, the Top 1% of on-peak load hours are also
analyzed as a separate period. Each calculation of market shares and market concentration
reflects average conditions (e.g., average loads) during one of the relevant study periods during
the year (e.g., Summer Peak). 2

        The study examines three periods within each market condition: off-peak, low peak,
and spike. Plant availability (see Section III.A.4 below) varies among these three categories.

               4.      Adjustments to Generating Capability

       The generating capability figures used for each period are obtained by multiplying the
seasonal capabilities by an availability factor, which is based on the period, unit location, and
NERC Generating Availability Data Systems (GADS) category of the unit. Data from 2019
through 2023 were used because those were the latest available on the NERC web site as of
August 2025. The GADS database provides national average operating information for
generating units by unit type and size range. For example, it provides data for coal-fired steam
units with capacities between 300 MW and 399 MW.

       For each period and each generating unit, the availability factor adjusts for the
following.

                       a)      Unplanned outage rates by GADS category
       For a given GADS category, the study assumes that unplanned (forced) outage rates
(as a share of generating capability available after allowing for planned outages) are constant


                                             Page 4
 across seasons and generating units, regardless of owner. Based on GADS data for 2019-2023,
the study calculates an equivalent forced outage rate (EIFOR), which measures the share of
generating capability in a GADS category that is not available because of forced outages. The
computation is EIFOR = (FOH)/AH, where FOH is number of forced outage hours and AH is
total hours available for generation after planned outages (but before forced outages). 5

                         b)       Planned outage rates by GADS category and season
       With some exceptions (for hydro, pumped storage, wind, and solar units), the study
assumes that the planned outage rate is constant for all generating units for a given GADS
category, area, and season. For a given GADS category, the share of hours of generating
capability that is not available as a result of planned outages is computed as (POH +
POEH)/PH; where PH are the period hours, POH are the hours not available because of planned
outages, and POEH are the hours not available because of planned outage extensions.

       Based upon planned outages during monthly peak hours each season reported in FERC
Form 714 by BAA, 6 the annual outage percentage is allocated to each season. Because outages
are likely to be “managed” to minimize disruptions, 7 the average planned outage rates during
peak periods by season are adjusted. Specifically, the planned outage rate for summer season
is set to 0. 8 In winter, instead of taking the seasonal average, we take the lowest level of
planned during the three winter months. For Spring/Fall, we used the average of the planned.

 IV.      Load for AEC Calculations

         The report uses estimates of load obligations from information available from public
sources such as FERC Form 714 and EIA Form 861. The calculation is performed in four steps.
First, the hours in each period are identified based on time and load level for the destination
market NWMT. Second, load “shapes” are calculated so that the annual load level in EIA 861
data can be translated into a load amount during each of the ten periods. Third, the annual
loads served by state and balancing area are then merged with the shapes to give the expected
load level served in each period. Fourth, when actual hourly load data for an entity are
available (e.g., from Form 714), we use the actual hourly load data. Finally, an “obligation”
amount is applied to each of the calculated load levels. Operational reserves are added to load
when calculating AEC. NorthWestern Energy’s load data was provided by the company.
